examples.label: OSCP Ch16 - get PSReadline history file path (survives Clear-History)

notes:
=== PowerShell History File - Credential Hunting ===
PSReadLine writes every PowerShell command to a plaintext file - credentials often captured verbatim.

=== TECHNICAL BACKGROUND ===
PSReadLine: enabled by default from PowerShell 5.0 on Windows 10
Writes every command entered at PS prompt to plaintext history file
Persists across sessions (all commands from all previous PS sessions in same file)
File location varies by user: C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt

=== COMMANDS ===
Get current user's history file path:
  (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath

Sweep all users' history files (requires read access to their profiles):
  foreach($user in ((ls C:\Users).fullname)){$f="$user\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt";if((Test-Path $f)){gc $f}}

Search history for credentials:
  Get-Content (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath | Select-String "password|pass|cred|secret|key"

=== WHAT TO SEARCH FOR ===
net use commands: net use \\server\share /user:domain\user Password123
Inline passwords passed to wevtutil, psexec, invoke-command:
  Invoke-Command -ComputerName DC01 -Credential (Get-Credential) → captures what was typed
Database connections with inline credentials
API keys and secrets in curl/Invoke-WebRequest calls
runas /user:DOMAIN\user - may have password typed immediately after

=== CHAINING CONTEXT ===
PS history → service account passwords → lateral movement to other hosts
PS history → domain admin running backup scripts inline → immediate privilege escalation
PS history + local admin → sweep ALL user histories on system → compound credential harvest
After privesc: re-run sweep against all user profiles → all users' credentials

=== WHAT TO LOOK FOR ===
PSReadLine enabled by default on Win10+ → almost always present
Large organizations with scripted admin tasks = high yield (admins run commands manually)
History files persist even after logoff/reboot - old credentials from months ago may still be valid
Also check: $env:APPDATA\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadLine\ConsoleHost_history.txt Also covered in: OSCP PEN-200 Chapter 16 (Windows Privilege Escalation).

recommended.note: Decrypt any Export-Clixml creds you find referenced.

name: Credential Hunting - PowerShell History
description: PSReadLine saves every PowerShell command to a per-user history file that often contains plaintext passwords passed on the command line. Read your own and, if accessible, every user's.

defense.why_it_works: PSReadLine saves all PowerShell commands typed in an interactive session to ConsoleHost_history.txt. Administrators often type commands with inline credentials (net use, Invoke-WebRequest with -Credential, custom scripts). This file is readable by the account owner and sometimes by other users if permissions are not restricted.
defense.prerequisites: Shell access as the target user, or read access to their history file. PSReadLine module loaded (default in PS5+).
defense.impact: Discovery of credentials, server names, scripts, and operational commands previously typed by the user - often including admin passwords passed inline to commands.
defense.detection: Read access to ConsoleHost_history.txt by a different process than PowerShell. PowerShell command enumerating all users' history files (foreach loop across C:\Users).
defense.artifacts: File access audit: ConsoleHost_history.txt read by non-PowerShell process | Process log: PowerShell foreach loop across all users' history files
defense.splunk_spl:
index=sysmon EventCode=11 TargetFilename="*ConsoleHost_history.txt"
| where NOT match(Image, "(?i)powershell")
| table _time, Computer, Image, TargetFilename

index=wineventlog EventCode=4104 ScriptBlockText="*ConsoleHost_history*"
| table _time, Computer, User, ScriptBlockText
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceFileEvents
| where FileName =~ "ConsoleHost_history.txt"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !has "powershell"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| sort by Timestamp desc
defense.sigma_rules: file_access_psreadline_history (PSReadLine history read by non-PowerShell process)
defense.prevention: Configure PSReadLine to not save history: Set-PSReadLineOption -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing. Never pass credentials inline in PowerShell commands - use PSCredential objects. Set history file permissions to owner-only (700 equivalent).
defense.misconfiguration: Default PSReadLine saves all typed commands. Administrators type credentials inline: `net use \\server /user:admin Password123!`. History file left at default permissions readable by other local users.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# PowerShell history contains credentials:
gc (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath
# Contains: net use \\DC01\SYSVOL /user:inlanefreight\admin P@ssw0rd2024!

# Enumerate all users' histories:
foreach($user in ((ls C:\users).fullname)){cat "$user\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\PowerShell\PSReadline\ConsoleHost_history.txt" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue}
defense.secure_config:
# Disable history saving (per user)
Set-PSReadLineOption -HistorySaveStyle SaveNothing

# Or restrict history file permissions
$histPath = (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath
icacls $histPath /inheritance:r /grant "$env:USERNAME:(R,W)"

# Never pass credentials as inline command arguments
$cred = Get-Credential  # prompts securely instead
defense.evasion: Copy the credential store (browser Login Data, .kdbx, PSReadline history) and decrypt/crack it OFFLINE rather than running signatured binaries (LaZagne/SharpChrome) on the host; scope searches to likely paths to limit disk I/O; use built-in cmdlets over dropped tools.

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review PowerShell Script Block / Module Logs, Sysmon for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Check for credential dumping artifacts (LSASS access, SAM hive reads, Kerberos anomalies)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

variations.label: All users' history
variations.description: Lists files in user profile directories. User home folders contain browser data, SSH keys, credential files, and application configs with stored passwords.

explain:
Reads the PSReadLine history file, which often holds passwords typed on the command line:
  gc (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath   print your own console history
The variation reads every user's ConsoleHost_history.txt under C:\Users\*\...\PSReadline\ - credentials passed as arguments to scripts/cmdlets frequently sit there in cleartext.
